title: His own way (Proverbs 22:6)
hookLine: train a child "in the way he should go"; commentators read it as each child's own way

cards: Two kids, same house, same parents, same bedtime story read the same way. One wants to hear it again and again. The other has already wandered off to take the radio apart.
The same lesson can land on one and slide right off the other. Proverbs has a well-known verse about training children. Read quickly, it sounds like a rule for everyone.
Read slowly, in Hebrew, it might be saying something else.

teach.b: In the King James words: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it." It sounds simple: pick the right path, put the child on it, and hold them there until it sticks.

teach.h: AL PI DARKO: ACCORDING TO HIS WAY.
teach.b: But the phrase translated in the way he should go is, word for word, closer to according to his way. Al pi darko. His way.

Whose way is that? Some commentators read it as the way a child ought to go, the path set out for everyone. Others notice that little his and read it as the child's own way: his nature, his pace, the shape of his mind.
Teach each child according to who that child is. The one who wants the story again and the one taking the radio apart may both learn, but not by the same road.
Another layer: the verb for train is chanokh, and elsewhere the Tanakh uses it for dedicating a new house.
So training a child, on this reading, is less like pushing and more like a beginning, opening something and setting it on its way.

teach.h: HE WILL NOT DEPART FROM IT.
teach.b: Then the promise: when he is old, he will not depart from it. On the second reading, the promise has a reason inside it: a way that was the child's own from the start is a way the child can keep.
The verse doesn't settle which reading is right, and Jewish teachers have held both.

how: Jewish teachers and parents quote Proverbs 22:6, reading 'according to his way' as a reason to teach each child in a way that fits that child.

o: his way: possibly each child's own road
his teacher: the one who trains a child
darkness: the hard years before wisdom

games.q: each child's own way — tap the pairs.
p: he will not depart from it

s: the Hebrew says, word for word, 'in the way he should go'
it is closer to 'according to his way'; 'should' is the translator's reading.
the verb for train is also used for dedicating a new house
chanokh: training as a kind of beginning.
Jewish teachers agree on one reading of 'his way'
some read it as the right road for all, others as the child's own way.

games.q: you're a teacher. one child learns by listening, the other by taking things apart. the verse says 'according to his way.' what do you do?
o: teach both the same way, to be fair.
fit the teaching to each child.
games.why: on the reading that 'his way' is the child's own, each one is taught by the road that fits them.

practice: Bring to mind one person you teach or explain things to, a child, a student, a new coworker, a parent learning a phone, and ask how they actually learn: by doing, asking, watching, or hearing a story?
Let one small change come to mind that would meet them on their road instead of yours. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: Darko. His way, the phrase from Proverbs that might mean the right road for all, or each child's own. Today's word.
